sec.title: Background and Objective
sec.p: Despite treatment advances, treatment resistance for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) is nearly universal. We studied the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetic properties of the combination of enzalutamide and cabazitaxel in patients with mCRPC. For phase 1, we examined the safety of combination therapy and determined the recommended phase 2 dose. Phase 2 primary endpoint included the percentage of patients achieving a ≥ 90% PSA decline (PSA90) as a measure of response to therapy.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A phase 1/2 single-arm, multi-institutional clinical trial enrolled adults with histologically confirmed progressive mCRPC without prior docetaxel or cabazitaxel chemotherapy for mCRPC. Co-administration of enzalutamide 160 mg orally once daily, cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 IV once every 21 days, and prednisone 5 mg orally twice daily in mCRPC. Descriptive statistical analysis was used for all primary and secondary endpoints. Estimated proportions are with 95% confidence interval using the exact method.

sec.title: Key Findings
sec.p: The study met its primary endpoint with 61.1% (95% CI, 43.5% to 76.9%) of patients achieving PSA90. Observed toxicities were similar to those seen with either agent alone.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The combination of enzalutamide and cabazitaxel exhibited robust activity with tolerable side effects. Chemo-hormonal therapies warrant further study in mCRPC.

sec.title: What Does the Study Add
sec.p: This study of enzalutamide and cabazitaxel combination therapy in patients with advanced, pre-treated mCRPC showed promising efficacy, indicating strong rationale for further investigation.

sec.title: Patient Summary
sec.p: In this report we looked at outcomes for patients with metastatic prostate cancer treated at multiple institutions with enzalutamide and cabazitaxel at the same time after castration therapy alone had stopped working. We found the combination was safe and had anti-cancer effect, warranting further investigation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Metastatic prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death among men in the United States.1,2 Therapies improving survival for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) include taxane chemotherapy, next-generation androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSI), radiopharmaceuticals, immunotherapy, poly ADP-ribose polymerase inhibitors, and checkpoint inhibitors. Treatment response rates and duration of response remain modest, necessitating further study to amplify response and extend overall survival.

Two smaller studies combining taxane chemotherapy with abiraterone in mCRPC showed evidence of synergy. Slovin and colleagues published their phase 2 non-comparative trial with two arms: Abiraterone with a switch to cabazitaxel upon progression versus the combination of cabazitaxel plus abiraterone upfront.3 While not powered to compare regimens, the combination arm showed 92.1% of patients achieved a PSA reduction of ≥50% from baseline (PSA50). Another study by Massard et al. tested the combination of cabazitaxel and abiraterone and showed manageable safety evidence of anti-tumor effect.4 The current study of cabazitaxel in combination with enzalutamide permitting prior chemotherapy and abiraterone in the setting of metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.

We hypothesized there would be a synergistic effect with combining cabazitaxel and enzalutamide in the mCRPC setting, allowing for prior docetaxel or abiraterone. Here, we report results of a phase 1/2 trial of cabazitaxel plus enzalutamide in patients with mCRPC who had not previously received chemotherapy or enzalutamide in the mCRPC setting.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: The trial design was approved by the institutional review boards of the Oregon Health & Science University, the University of Washington, and the VA Portland Health Care System. Written informed consent was obtained from all patients prior to enrollment. The data generated in this study are available upon request from the corresponding author and is registered on clinicaltrials.gov as NCT02522715.

sec.title: Patient population
sec.p: We enrolled patients who were ≥18 years of age with histologically confirmed progressive mCRPC who had not received docetaxel or cabazitaxel chemotherapy for mCRPC prostate cancer. Prior docetaxel in the mCRPC or mHSPC setting was permitted if the cancer did not progress on chemotherapy and >6 months had elapsed since completion of docetaxel. Prior therapy with abiraterone was allowed, but participants must not have received an alternative androgen pathway modulator. Prior immunotherapy (sipuleucel-T) was allowed. Eligible patients must have had evidence of prostate cancer progression biochemically or radiographically. ECOG performance status of 0-1 and adequate organ function were required. Key exclusion criteria included a history or predisposal to seizures, uncontrolled diabetes, symptomatic congestive heart failure, unstable angina, and cardiac arrhythmia.

sec.title: Study design and treatment
sec.p: This was a single-arm, open-label, multi-center phase 2 study with a phase 1 dose de-escalation of cabazitaxel, enzalutamide, and prednisone for mCRPC without prior chemotherapy treatment in the mHSPC setting. The phase 1 dose de-escalation began with full doses: cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 IV every 3 weeks and enzalutamide 160 mg daily, along with standard ADT and prednisone 5 mg twice daily. All patients received granulocyte-stimulating growth factor (eg GCSF) per institutional standard. Toxicity was evaluated according to NCI CTCAEv4. Dose limiting toxicity was assessed during cycles 1 and 2 and defined as: grade 3-4 non-hematologic toxicity, >21-day delay of next cycle due to toxicity, hematologic toxicity of grade 3 neutropenia with fever, grade 3-4 neutropenia >7 days or through day 1 of the subsequent cycle, or grade 3-4 thrombocytopenia with significant bleeding. If none of the initial 3 patients experienced dose limiting toxicity, the dose-finding phase was complete, and cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 would be used. If 1 of 3 experienced a dose-limiting toxicity, 3 more would be enrolled at that dose. If 2 of 6 experienced a dose-limiting toxicity, cabazitaxel was reduced to 20 mg/m2 and 3-6 more subjects were enrolled. If ≥2 dose-limiting toxicities were observed, the trial would be terminated.

Patients in phase 2 received the cabazitaxel dose from phase 1 on day 1 of 21-day cycles, prednisone 5 mg twice daily, enzalutamide 160 mg daily starting on day 1 with continued castration. After 6-10 cycles, patients could continue enzalutamide monotherapy with 28-day cycles. Cabazitaxel reduction to 20 mg/m2 was allowed if toxicity occurred, further reductions were not permitted. The use of bisphosphonate or denosumab was permitted. Patients were treated until progression, unacceptable adverse event(s), withdrawal, or investigator discretion.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic assessments
sec.p: Pharmacokinetic parameters of cabazitaxel with and without enzalutamide were assessed in the phase 1 and 7 phase II patients. For cycle 2, samples were drawn pre-infusion and at 0.5, 1 (coinciding with the end of the infusion), 1.5, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours.

Plasma concentration-time data were used to calculate pharmacokinetic parameters by noncompartmental analysis (Phoenix WinNonlin, Certara, Princeton, NJ). Maximum plasma concentrations (Cmax) are the observed values. Area under the plasma concentration-time curve from time zero until 24 hours (AUC0-24) was calculated by the linear trapezoidal rule. The terminal elimination rate constant (lz) from regression analysis of terminal points was used to calculate half-life (T1/2.= ln2/lz).

sec.title: Efficacy assessments
sec.p: The primary outcome of phase 2 was percentage of patients achieving ≥90% PSA decline from baseline (PSA90) at any time. Secondary outcomes included adverse events, a PSA50 decline, and tumor response per RECIST 1.1 and Prostate Cancer Working Group 2 (PCWG2) PFS criteria.5 A secondary exploratory analysis assessed differences in PSA response stratified by prior abiraterone exposure. Baseline metastatic tissue biopsies were collected for biomarker research. Safety data were collected on all patients and defined per CTCAE v4.0.6

sec.title: Exploratory objectives
sec.p: Optional metastatic biopsies were performed upon progression. To investigate tumor microenvironment changes, spatial transcriptomic profiling on paired bone biopsy samples from one patient before and after progression on enzalutamide was performed. Clustering based on gene expression was analyzed in the post-progression sample. Further analysis of additional biopsies is ongoing.

sec.title: Statistical considerations
sec.p: The AFFIRM study showed enzalutamide resulted in 24.8% of patients achieving a PSA90 in post-docetaxel, which was used for sample size calculation.7 Based on this, the null hypothesis conveyed 25% of patients would achieve a PSA90, with an alternative assumption of 50%. This keeps in mind that the patient population in this trial would consist of more heavily pre-treated patients and patients harboring biologically more aggressive prostate cancer. A total of 33 subjects were needed to achieve 82% power using one-sample binomial method for a 2-sided alpha of 0.05.

Descriptive statistical analysis was used for all primary and secondary endpoints. Estimated proportions are with 95% confidence interval (CI) using the exact method. One-sample binomial test assessed whether the proportion achieving ≥90% PSA decline from baseline is significantly different from 0.25. As an exploratory subgroup analysis, various PSA response rates were estimated in prior abiraterone vs. naïve subgroups. Using Kaplan-Meier, median overall survival, median PFS, and median radiographic PFS were estimated with 95% CIs. Median follow-up was calculated as the midpoint and reported with a range. Statistical analysis was performed using R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing. A P-value < .05 was statistically significant unless otherwise indicated.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics and study drug exposure
sec.p: Between November 24, 2015, and April 4, 2019, 37 patients with mCRPC were enrolled at 3 centers. Baseline characteristics are in Table 1. Three participants enrolled in phase 1 dose de-escalation and 32 into phase 2 efficacy analysis. One patient withdrew before receiving study treatment, and another withdrew from the study before post-treatment PSA or imaging. Therefore, 35 patients were evaluable for PFS analysis, 36 for safety, and 32 underwent on-trial imaging. The median number of enzalutamide cycles was 16.5 (range 2-47), and cabazitaxel cycles was 9 (range 2-10). Seventeen patients (47%) completed all 10 cabazitaxel cycles.

sec.title: Phase 1 results
sec.p: Three patients completed at least 2 cycles of cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2, enzalutamide 160 mg daily, and prednisone 5 mg twice daily. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred. Therefore, the dose of cabazitaxel, 25 mg/m2 was chosen for the trial.

sec.title: Phase 2 efficacy analyses
sec.p: As pre-specified, all 3 of the phase 1 patients were included in the phase 2 efficacy analysis. Sixty-three percent (22/35 patients, 95% CI, 44.9% to 78.5%) met the primary endpoint, rejecting the null hypothesis (P < .001). Eighty percent (28/35 patients, 80.0% 95% CI, 63.1% to 91.6%) achieved PSA50. (Table 2, Figure S1) Twenty-eight patients underwent on-trial imaging; radiographic response rate was 50% (95% CI, 30.6-69.4), complete response 10.7% (95% CI, 2.3-28.2), stable disease 42.9% (95% CI, 24.5-62.8), and progression 7% (95% CI, 0.9-23.5) (Table 2). Using a data cutoff of June 28, 2022, median follow-up was 23.7 months (range: 4.9 to 62.4). No subjects were still receiving enzalutamide at the time of data cut-off. Median overall survival was 25.1 months (95% CI: 19.4 to 37.6). Median PSA progression free survival was 11.9 months (95% CI, 9.2-15.4), and the median radiographic progression free survival was 22.2 months (95% CI, 13.6-25.2) (Figure 1).

sec.p: Nine patients received prior abiraterone, of whom 2 (22%) achieved PSA50 and 1 (11.1%) achieved PSA90 as compared to 26 patients who were abiraterone-naïve, of whom all 26 (100%) achieved PSA50 (P < .001), and 19 (73.1%) of the abiraterone-naïve patients achieved PSA90 (P = .002). Among the 7 patients with prior docetaxel in the hormone-naïve setting, 6 (85.7%) achieved PSA90.

sec.title: Safety and adverse events
sec.p: Seven of 36 patients (19%) required cabazitaxel 20 mg/m2 dose reductions. Three discontinued for adverse events, including one for possible seizure. Six patients remained on enzalutamide at data cutoff. Overall, the combination was well tolerated. (Table 3). Most of the treatment-related adverse events were grade 1-2. Common treatment-related adverse events were fatigue (67%), nausea (47%), peripheral neuropathy (44%), diarrhea (42%), and dysgeusia (28%). Twenty-five percent (9/36 patients) experienced grade 3 adverse events, hypertension, febrile neutropenia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, failure to thrive, fracture, fatigue, and anemia. Two patients (5.6%) had febrile neutropenia. No grade 4-5 treatment-related adverse events occurred.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic analysis
sec.p: Pharmacokinetic studies were performed in 9 patients. Eight patients received cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 for 2 cycles, 1 received cabazitaxel 25 mg/m2 in cycle 1 and 20 mg/m2 in cycle 2. One patient had only cycle 1 data and was excluded. Of cabazitaxel pharmacokinetic measures (Cmax, AUC0-24h, T1/2), only Cmax significantly decreased with enzalutamide (Table S1).
PK studies also showed reduced cabazitaxel AUC in several patients with 1 patient’s samples demonstrating an 81% decline, persisting after normalization to dose (Figure S2).

sec.title: Preliminary correlative results
sec.p: Following enzalutamide, progression biopsies showed increased myeloid infiltration and reduced epithelial cell content (Figure S3). Post-treatment biopsy revealed upregulation of inflammatory and proliferative genes (eg MKI67, CXCL12, S100A9) and reduction of prostate epithelial lineage markers (eg AR, KLK3, ACPP) (Figure S4). Enrichment analysis demonstrated activation of lineage plasticity, neuroendocrine differentiation, and cytokine signaling pathways.
Together, these findings suggest progression on enzalutamide is associated with immune remodeling and the emergence of a distinct plastic tumor niche. Further analysis of biopsy tissue is ongoing.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Findings from this phase 1/2 trial of concurrent cabazitaxel, prednisone, and enzalutamide in patients with mCRPC demonstrate that the treatment combination was tolerable and had robust activity. Overall, the side effects that patients experienced were similar to those reported for either cabazitaxel or enzalutamide alone—with fatigue, nausea, and neuropathy as the 3 most common toxicities of any grade.

The combination of cabazitaxel and enzalutamide may have an additive or synergistic PSA response rate compared to either agent alone, although cross-trial comparisons are very difficult due to several unmeasured confounders. The PSA50 response was 39.2% in the TROPIC trial of cabazitaxel after docetaxel and 68.7% in the FIRSTANA trial of cabazitaxel prior to docetaxel.8,9 The PSA50 response with the combination was notably higher than each of these at 77.8%. In the PREVAIL trial of enzalutamide prior to docetaxel,7 a ≥ 90% PSA response was seen in 47% of patients, compared to 61% with the combination tested in this study. Data regarding other studies of cabazitaxel with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor in the mCRPC setting also include 2 Ph1/2 studies of cabazitaxel with abiraterone3,4 and the Ph3 CHAARTED2 (EA8153) study, which compared combination chemohormonal therapy with cabazitaxel and abiraterone vs abiraterone alone after docetaxel in the mCRPC setting and was well-tolerated and showed a PFS benefit, but not OS benefit, although the study was not powered for OS.10

PSA responses to the combination of cabazitaxel and enzalutamide were attenuated in patients previously treated with abiraterone. This is not unexpected, as patients previously treated with abiraterone are less likely to respond to enzalutamide, and vice versa.7,11 In a large study, a PSA50 response was observed in 27% of patients treated with enzalutamide who had received prior abiraterone, which is similar to the PSA50 response of 20% seen in our limited sample of patients with prior abiraterone exposure.12 These findings suggest that the combination may not be able to fully overcome resistance to abiraterone. Ultimately, the ideal sequence of therapies in mCRPC has yet to be defined and will likely depend on both patient- and tumor-specific factors. Finally, it is possible that the addition of prednisone in our study may have slightly impacted results, negatively or positively, but both the label and other studies with cabazitaxel include prednisone in the treatment regimen.

Additionally, an earlier analysis of 14 subjects receiving cabazitaxel and enzalutamide revealed decreased blood AUC0-24h cabazitaxel levels and a significantly different Cmax at day 1 of cycle 3 (cabazitaxel + enzalutamide) relative to day 1 of cycle 1 (cabazitaxel). Possible reasons for subtle differences between datasets include a smaller sample size, and cabazitaxel levels were tested at cycle 2 rather than cycle 3. In either case, these data indicate there is a likelihood of decreased cabazitaxel exposure during enzalutamide administration. Based on the Ph3 PROSELICA study, the 20 mg/m2 dosing of cabazitaxel was shown to be non-inferior to the 25 mg/m2 dosing.13 In our study, results for the combination were effective, thus, it is possible the lower cabazitaxel exposure was countered by the synergistic anti-tumor effect. However, this may also explain why patients who had received prior abiraterone had an attenuated response to the combination of cabazitaxel and enzalutamide. In other words, it is possible they not only effectively had a lower dose of cabazitaxel, but they may have lacked the benefit of androgen receptor modulation (given known cross-resistance between abiraterone and enzalutamide14).

Finally, combination therapy in newly diagnosed, metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer is now routine. While initial studies examined “doublet” therapies of androgen deprivation therapy plus docetaxel, enzalutamide, abiraterone apalutamide, and darolutamide, new studies are examining the effect of androgen deprivation therapy plus docetaxel with either darolutamide or abiraterone.15,16 These so-called “triplet” therapies show that androgen receptor signaling inhibitor in addition to docetaxel is superior to docetaxel alone at least in a significant proportion of patients. This suggests in settings of highly aggressive growth and disease progression, upfront chemohormonal therapy could be an effective approach in patients who have not recently been on androgen receptor signaling inhibitors, or taxane chemotherapy. With more therapeutic options such as targeted therapies, theranostics, and immunologic and bispecific antibodies in the pipeline, our study adds to other evidence that chemohormonal therapy remains an important option for metastatic prostate cancer. Limitations of our study include single-arm design (lack of randomization), moderate sample size, possible selection bias, and residual confounding.

In conclusion, the results from this study of the combination of cabazitaxel and enzalutamide demonstrated encouraging efficacy in an advanced, castrate-resistant, and pre-treated population. Results suggest that the combination of cabazitaxel and enzalutamide deserves further study.
